articles.title: Centrist Democrats Are Trying to Throw the Michigan Race
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: In Michigan, where progressive Abdul El-Sayed is facing off for the must-win Senate seat against Donald Trump–backed Mike Rogers, Democrats have a problem. How to reconcile their distaste for their own party’s nominee with the imperative to care about winning? Attorney General Dana Nessel modeled a way out of the bind with a comically backhanded endorsement. Tasked with trying to convince Jewish Democrats that they should vote for El-Sayed despite the blizzard of smears charging he’s a dangerous antisemite, Attorney General Dana Nessel offered the most unappetizing of unappetizing pitches. Referencing the biblical story of Queen Esther, who chose to put her life on the line to save many others, she implored those in the room to do the same. “It is perhaps up to us now to follow in her path and sacrifice the comfort, safety and security and even the very future of our own people in exchange for the opportunity to save the rest of humanity,” she told them. It’s hard to think of a more counterproductive call to action than this. In fact, it might even make you think that the speaker didn’t even want her audience to vote for the endorsed candidate, greater good be damned. You’d be in good company. Bernie Sanders, the country’s most prominent Jewish politician, recently told Politico he believed that some Democratic officials actively want El-Sayed to lose the race to the Republican Rogers. These Democrats, Sanders said, viewed progressive candidates like El-Sayed as “a threat” to continued “oligarchy,” to “neverending wars,” and to “continued support for the extremist [Benjamin] Netanyahu government in Israel,” and so figure, “maybe we should let them lose.” “You’re talking about a small number of people who are at the head of the Democratic Party. You’re talking about the donor class,” Sanders said. If, like Sanders, you’re also getting the sneaking suspicion that centrist Democrats are trying to throw the Michigan Senate race, you’re not crazy. Some of them are actually outright admitting it. No Bones About It Last week, a group of Michigan Democrats began circulating a letter announcing they would be voting for Rogers in November, because, in their words, “if El-Sayed were to win the general election in this important swing state, we fear the far left and anti-Jewish elements in the Democratic Party would become dominant, including in the imminent 2028 presidential race.” That letter has 412 signatures as of the time of writing. Another pro-Israel Michigander who usually votes Democrat, Ann Arbor Rabbi Asher Lopatin, put it even more starkly in an op-ed for Israeli newspaper Haaretz . “Some will argue, as I personally do, that the best thing for the Democrats and the progressive cause, in the long run, is to show that anti-Israel candidates like El-Sayed can’t win, thus bringing the Democratic Party back to its more traditional and pro-Israel stance,” he wrote. “A loss for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in November could save the Democratic Party from a hostile takeover ahead of the 2028 presidential election.” Another lifelong Democrat in the state, Detroit journalist Stacy Gittleman, made a similar declaration. “I will NOT be voting for Abdul, because he poses to me and many others as an extremist who, if he gets into office as a US senator, will spend all his time not pursuing ‘Medicare for all’ but bashing Israel and pursuing every energy to sever the alliance between the United States and Israel,” she wrote last week. (Gittleman recently complained to Fox News about all the Palestinian flags she saw at a party convention in April.) Meanwhile, former backers of El-Sayed’s centrist primary rival have reportedly appeared on a donor call with Rogers and his pollster, while three Democratic bundlers have hosted a fundraiser for the pro-Israel Rogers. It’s refreshing, in many ways, that these Democrats are just coming out and saying it: Yes, we would prefer that Democrats lose this key race so that our side stays in control of the party and maintains the party’s lockstep support for Israel, and we are actively working to make that happen . Given that this stance is totally contrary to the interests of Democrats’ own voters, who overwhelmingly share El-Sayed’s criticisms of Israeli policy and see their biggest priority as constraining Trump and the GOP, most centrist Democrats are not openly making these kinds of claims. But one gets the sense that some of them, like Nessel, are quietly on board. Before making her anti-pitch to the state’s Jewish Democrats, Nessel — maybe best known for trying to charge a group of antiwar student protesters with felonies last year before crying “antisemitism” when she faced pushback — had not exactly been helpful to her party’s candidate’s campaign. Last week, Nessel sat down for a conversation with former Iraq War propagandist David Frum, in which she paid lip service to the need to win the race against Rogers, but then spent the bulk of the interview attacking El-Sayed. Among other things, she charged that his criticism of Israel was “turning up the anti-Semitism,” and that he was “making excuses” for terrorism. In that same interview, she implied she might one day leave the party over its growing criticism of Israel. Similarly eyebrow-raising has been a host of centrist Democrats’ orientation toward Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, whom they allege to be a dangerous radical allied with El-Sayed. Over the past few weeks, Piker has been at the center of a somehow-still-ongoing news cycle that has entirely consumed coverage of the race — in turn driving up El-Sayed’s negatives, and benefiting his Republican opponent, who has avoided any similar scrutiny over a host of antisemitic and other unsavory associations and serious scandals , not least the fact that he actually did advocacy for an officially designated terrorist group while taking donations from its supporters. All of this is, to say the least, extremely unusual. Typically, when a party’s candidate comes under attack, members of that party will try their best to avoid the inciting issue and pivot to something else, like criticizing their opponent. Consider Rep. Debbie Dingell’s response to questions about Piker, whom she has said is irrelevant to the election and has declared she will refuse to answer questions about. When challenged on this during a CNN appearance, Dingell immediately pivoted to talking about affordability and to Trump and the GOP’s cuts to health care and food stamps before calling the Piker obsession a Republican attempt to distract and divide voters. This is the standard behavior of a politician who wants their candidate to win. By contrast, in Michigan, centrist Democrats and those aligned with them have seemed determined to do as much as they can to keep Piker front and center in the race, while appearing totally uninterested in training any fire on their rival party’s candidate. Just look at the ratio of tweets about Piker compared to tweets about Rogers from some of the Democrats most hostile to the Left. For Rep. Josh Gottheimer — the centrist Democrat aligned with the Wall Street–funded group Third Way who, following El-Sayed’s primary win, launched a campaign explicitly about attacking him and progressives like him — it’s a five-to-zero ratio. For Hillary Scholten, the Michigan Democrat refusing to back Piker after trying to sink him with accusations of misogyny in the primary, it’s two-to-zero. For Brad Sherman, cochair of the Congressional Israel Allies Caucus, it’s three-to-zero. But none of them hold a candle to Center for American Progress President Neera Tanden, who has notched up a four-to-one ratio of Piker-to-Rogers tweets since the primary, while also tweeting by far the most about him than any of these other figures. Bear in mind that this is a conservative count: it doesn’t include any of Tanden’s many replies to her own tweets and to others’ . Additionally, none of the tweets about Rogers are actually criticisms of the candidate — two are about how El-Sayed’s defeated centrist opponent polled better against him, while the other is an attack on the Left. Tweets are not by any means a scientific measure of someone’s thoughts or public utterances. But these numbers do give us a sense of some centrist Democrats’ overwhelming public fixation on Piker, and their lack of focus on the GOP candidate who potentially stands to beat their nominee. Meanwhile, as explicit calls to sabotage El-Sayed’s campaign get louder, those who a little over a month ago were wailing about the dangers of self-defeating “factionalism” suddenly don’t care. Matthew Yglesias, the centrist blogger aligned with the party’s corporate wing, has literally dozens of tweets bemoaning how the Left was engaged in a dangerous “factional” mission that put beating centrist Democrats ahead of defeating Trump and the GOP. Mind you, this was about left-wing candidates simply competing against centrist Democrats in primaries , when Trump and other Republicans weren’t even on the ballot. But now that it’s centrist, pro-Israel Democrats who are outright saying that they want the Republican to win the whole thing so they can come out on top in the factional intraparty war, even if it endangers a Democratic majority in the Senate, what is Yglesias’ response? He thinks “the whole leftist sabotage narrative is way overblown,” and that the Left should simply stop “lying” about this and point to all the centrist Democrats who are supporting El-Sayed instead. Far From Unprecedented If it sounds far-fetched that a contingent of centrist Democrats would try to deliberately tank the Michigan race, even at the cost of a Senate majority, it shouldn’t. After all, as Senate leader Chuck Schumer recently acknowledged , the Democrats can technically still win control of the upper chamber even if they lose that seat. It would also be far from unprecedented. In fact, it’s exactly what happened with the United Kingdom’s Labour Party at the end of last decade. It’s now a matter of public record that a group of centrist UK Labour officials concocted a well-funded plan to undermine the party’s leftist leader Jeremy Corbyn; that they manufactured an “antisemitism crisis” as one of the principal ways to do so; that they explicitly listed a future Labour government under Corbyn as an obstacle to their plans; and that their chosen strategy to do this was to try to take back control of the party after he lost a general election. An inquiry into the matter later found that, in the UK’s 2017 elections, centrist Labour officials secretly diverted resources away from Corbyn-aligned candidates fighting for “winnable seats.” When the party ended up having a much better showing on election night than expected, these officials were “silent and grey-faced,” with one senior Labour official describing the strong result as the “opposite to what I had been working towards for the last couple of years.” These kinds of calculations are hardly unique to British politics. As Amie Parnes and Jonathan Allen reported in their insiders’ account of the 2020 US election, centrist Democrats were torn about who they would vote for if that race came down to Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump, since “their fears of losing their party to socialism competed with their fears of Trump winning a second term.” Many Democratic voters would likely find it hard to believe prominent figures within their party are cynical enough to intentionally favor Trump and his allies if it meant winning the party’s faction fight. At least some have done them the favor of saying it explicitly, so there can be no mistake.

articles.title: The Dog Stars Is a Western in Postapocalyptic Drag
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: The dullest yet most enraging film of the year may very well be The Dog Stars , a draggy postapocalyptic thriller with no thrills, even of the grim dystopian kind. This latest effort by director Ridley Scott, from a screenplay by Mark L. Smith ( Twisters, The Revenant ) based on the 2012 novel of the same name by Peter Heller, is about the survivors of a flu pandemic who live in isolated enclaves defending their turf from marauding bands of desperate nomads. Jacob Elordi plays Hig, an ex-mechanic turned prop pilot whose last remaining relationship from the old days is with his dog, Jasper. Jasper is a cool dog, a Belgian Malinois, who keeps whining nervously as if he knows he’s not safe with Hig. They fly around Colorado in Hig’s little putt-putting plane, fetching supplies for Hig’s enclave and the nearby hilltop group of Mennonites led by the fatherly Aaron (Benedict Wong). Then it’s back home to the fort-like settlement with tough ex-Marine survivalist Bangley (Josh Brolin) as Hig’s only human company. A Man Well-Suited to the Apocalypse They’re not really friends though. “You like this,” as Hig puts it. “You were living like this ten years before it happened.” And it’s true, Bangley is well-suited to the postapocalyptic life. He looks most at ease up in the rudimentary watchtower, ready to gun down anybody who comes into their area. Mostly the trespassers are “just kids,” though they might be flu-ridden kids, and they’re certainly looking for food in an age of scarcity, so Bangley shoots them dead regardless. Though he’s really waiting for worthier opponents — a fifty-man gang of tattooed, knife-wielding skinheads howling for blood, say — who inevitably arrive. When they do, he’s armed and ready for them, and mutters, “’Bout time.” Bangley’s attitude toward Hig is no more complimentary, though he’s adamant they should stick together in their two-man camp for the sake of their own survival. Hig is a brooding hunk who’s always distracted by the idea that civilization must be back up and fully functioning somewhere out there. After picking up repeated radio signals, he’s convinced that place is Grand Junction, Colorado. He’s fixated on flying his plane there, a precarious journey into the savage unknown based on what might be decoy signals to lure in fresh supply-bearing prey. Bangley calls Hig a “consistently stupid bastard,” and he’s not wrong. It’s hard not to feel massively impatient with Hig, who’s lost in nostalgia for his late wife and old ways and can’t seem to stop risking the lives of the few who are left. If Hig takes off, that leaves Bangley entirely on his own, plus the Mennonites don’t have any access to outside-world supplies either. As for Jasper, well. . . . don’t ask. That dog knew he was in big trouble with Hig. We’re seeing the limits of Jacob Elordi’s acting ability and star quality here. He should never again play a depressed person wandering around lost in his own inner turmoil, because he really doesn’t do it well. He just looks handsome and mopey. Of course, Hig flies off regardless of anybody else and winds up crashing his plane almost immediately. He finds an enclave in the woods featuring another crusty stand-your-ground, shoot-first old guy named Jack (Guy Pearce), an ex–Navy SEAL. Jack’s getting along by subsistence farming with his daughter Cima (Margaret Qualley), a widow and former medical student, and one lone donkey, another doomed animal you have to feel bad about. Cima persuades Jack, aka “Pops,” not to kill Hig, presumably because he’s the only hot young male left alive. So instead they help Hig fix his plane as well as clear a runway for it through the trees. This requires cutting down pines and pulling up their stumps. It was while Jack and Hig were working together to uproot one stump that I suddenly remembered the epic stump-clearing scene from the old 1953 Western Shane . And that’s around when the movie turns into a retro-Western, the one featuring lone gunslingers and tough ranchers laying down their weapons and working together to clear the land and make the wilderness into a garden. And of course, they’ll have to clear the land of heathens too, so very soon their little homestead is threatened by a shrieking band of face-painted warriors on horseback. Once you know what kind of fantasy you’re in, the rest decodes itself. This is the one that pretends to be dismally postapocalyptic but doesn’t actually mourn the loss of civilization at all, as you see when you meet its chief representative, Allison Janney as Darlene, a sadistic sicko in a stewardess uniform acting as the dictator of an airport enclave. Who wants to go back to that when you can return to the restored wilderness as a heroic white settler in the world where men are men again, fulfilling their Manifest Destiny, and women appreciate them properly? When you can start all over again with tons of land to spread out on and all the resources that the deceased population of the world won’t be needing anymore? A Western Neverland You know that famous scene in the John Ford Western My Darling Clementine (1946), when Wyatt Earp, all duded up, goes to an open-air dance on the newly constructed floor of the unfinished church and dances awkwardly but charmingly with the idealized young lady of refinement? And the whole town of Tombstone is there to participate in the refounding of a Western Neverland version of the United States, freed of the more corrupting influences of Europe and the urbanized multiracial East Coast? Yep, it’s redone here. There’s an open-air dance at the Mennonite enclave — which motivates the proper Western iconography of nineteenth-century work clothing, with wide-brimmed hats and all — that unites all the survivors of the former enclaves, Hig and Bangley, Jack and Cima. John Ford at his corniest wouldn’t go as far as this scene does in celebrating the lovable neo-pioneers. Even Bangley, the avid killer, is revealed to be a delightful scamp in the end, picking up a guitar to play with the little band of local musicians that sprang up out of nowhere to play an old-timey dance tune for the stomping, grinning locals. The Dog Stars is bombing at the box office, as the public quite rightly avoids it like the plague. At this point in our history, this kind of revanchist shit is just unforgivable.

articles.title: The Scandal That Could Break the Latin American Far Right
articles.author: Kurt Hackbarth
articles.content: On Tuesday, August 18, an Argentine citizen named Fernando Cerimedo was arrested at the Viru Viru International Airport in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia. Cerimedo, age forty-five, was charged with the attempted homicide of his ex-partner, Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller, and ordered held for 180 days of pretrial detention. The details are grisly: security camera footage showed hit men, disguised as delivery workers, firing on an unsuspecting Beller at point-blank range before fleeing the scene. Compounding matters, Beller, who miraculously survived the assault, was apparently pregnant with Cerimedo’s own child. Thus far, the affair could be classified as a case — gruesome, yes, but hardly unusual — of a botched femicide in the wake of a failed relationship. Something to briefly grace the crime section of the local papers. And indeed, that is how a number of interested parties would be keen to frame it. But Cerimedo happens to be the disinformation mastermind behind the far-right campaigns that have taken Latin America by storm. Nor are his connections limited to the Southern Cone: they extend up into the inner circles of Trumpism itself. Cerimedo Is at the Center of the Latin American Far Right Once you start looking at the Latin American far right, Fernando Cerimedo’s name starts popping up everywhere. He was in Brazil, helping the Bolsonaros spread the narrative of fraud in the 2022 elections that saw the return of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He was in Argentina, where — according to Beller — he worked for the very Javier Milei he considered “crazy” all while compiling information on the bribery scandal involving Milei’s sister, Karina, the secretary general of the presidency. He was in Chile, where he bragged about tanking the referendum for the new constitution that would have replaced the Augusto Pinochet–era version still in force while reportedly also assisting in the presidential campaign of José Antonio Kast. He was in Peru, hanging with a close adviser to Keiko Fujimori in the run-up to the June presidential elections she won by a hair’s breadth. He was in Honduras, where he purportedly appears on audio admitting to electoral crimes in the November 2025 elections that saw the surprise victory of Donald Trump ally Nasry Asfura. And he was in the Colombian presidential elections , where, according to the official count, another pro-Trumper, Abelardo de la Espriella, defeated Iván Cepeda by less than 1 percentage point in June. Why was he in such high demand? Because Cerimedo was the guy who could put it all together. Political marketing. Audience targeting. Farms of bots numbering into the hundreds of thousands. Deceptive polling. Opposition research. Artificial intelligence manipulations. In short, he supplied the negative message — lie or slander — then segmented, sensationalized, and amplified it to reach the largest and most receptive audience possible. Together with his partner, the serial falsifier Javier Negre (repeatedly sentenced in Spain for fabricating information and even entire interviews ), they founded La Derecha Diario , the online media platform designed to launder this material in the form of “news” across all of Latin America. Beginning in Argentina, the outlet quickly established regional editions in Mexico, Uruguay, Ecuador, Israel, and an English version in the United States, where Negre would become a regular fixture at White House press conferences. In the case of Mexico, as Negre himself explained at a Conservative Political Action Conference event, the outfit was invited to set up shop by far-right magnate Ricardo Salinas Pliego in order to “wage the cultural battle.” Mexico, Beller contends — a starting point for interfering in the country’s 2027 midterm elections — was next on his list. All of the above fueled by a network of digital wallets found on his phone totaling some $132.8 million . A Minister Without Portfolio But nothing beats Bolivia, where Cerimedo was far more than a digital hit man: he functioned as a sort of all-powerful minister without portfolio in the right-wing government of Rodrigo Paz, elected in October 2025 following a devastating fracture in the ruling Movement Toward Socialism (MAS) party. Although they were careful to keep him off the official payroll, the “principal adviser” wielded what amounted practically to co-governance powers in communications, the cabinet, and the police. So great was this power that, in the days leading up to the attempt on Beller’s life, Cerimedo was in contact via chat with Lieutenant Colonel Erik Correa González, director of intelligence for Bolivia’s Special Anti-Narcotics Force, to coordinate the assault. Correa is also under investigation for allegedly receiving bribes of $50,000 per plane to turn a blind eye to cocaine flights. For his part, and in addition to attempted homicide, Cerimedo is also being investigated for illicit enrichment via a drug connection , specifically the trafficking of controlled substances and the covering up of drug trafficking. It is the irony of ironies. Cerimedo’s disinformation machine specialized in attaching the prefix narco to progressive leaders, movements, and governments up and down the region in order to discredit them. Now he stands accused not only of colluding with narcos himself but of using one of them to try to off his own former partner and unborn child. Every accusation is a confession. The US Connection If the Cerimedo story ended here, that might at least partially justify the dearth of coverage in the English-language press. But it does not. According to an investigation published in the Mexican daily La Jornada and based on documents filed under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), Cerimedo’s port of entry into the United States was Miami. The South Florida city was more than a business address; it operated “as a platform for coordination among Latin American campaigns, ideologically driven media outlets, political consultants, organizations within the Cuban American ecosystem, and sectors of the Republican Party with the ability to influence U.S. policy toward the hemisphere.” And the key welcome-wagon figure in this extremist petri dish is Damian Merlo, a lobbyist, public relations consultant, managing partner at the Latin America Advisory Group (LAAG), and former screening officer for the US Department of State in Havana. It was Merlo, in fact, who organized the viral appearance of Javier Milei on the Tucker Carlson program in 2023, two months before his election as president of Argentina. For Cerimedo, Merlo could offer access to the offices of congresspeople deeply involved in hard-right politics in Latin America, such as Representatives Mario Díaz-Balart and Maria Elvira Salazar — who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere — and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Indeed, in an official State Department photo of the Shield of the Americas summit on March 7, 2026, Cerimedo is seated next to Rodrigo Paz and across from the US secretary of state at a chummy table of six. When, in that same 2023, Cerimedo established his company Numen Publicidad in Miami, Numen and LAAG joined forces to work on the Milei campaign. Numen also brought Cerimedo together with a fundamental person in this entire saga: Brad Parscale , digital media director for Trump 2016 and campaign manager for Trump 2020. It was a match made in heaven , as the two offered a very similar basket of “services”: it was Parscale who paid some $6 million to Cambridge Analytica in 2016 to harness Facebook data harvested from eighty-seven million users without their consent. In the Honduran elections, Parscale advised Numen remotely about leveraging data to target voters. In Bolivia, he went one better, traveling to the country to help Numen’s team harness his companies’ data tools. In 2025, Cerimedo was designated representative and exclusive Latin American licensee of Campaign Nucleus, owned by Parscale, and EyesOver, an affiliated company. “Brad provided all the technology I work with,” Cerimedo has admitted. In October 2025, Parscale registered under FARA with the Israeli government, through the intermediary of Havas Media Germany GmbH. The House of Cards Tariffs, boat bombings, open interventionism, the kidnapping of a sitting head of state: even a cursory review of the second Trump administration’s onslaught on Latin America and the Caribbean is enough to drive anyone to desperation. But as the Cerimedo affair demonstrates, the far-right barrage is more fragile than it may at first appear. From Kast to Milei to Paz, the leaders elected under the wave have, in quick succession, become unpopular, run into scandal, faced popular protest, or all of the above. Victories in Honduras, Peru, and Colombia were razor-thin, ripe for being upended by the type of manipulation contracted in the North and metastasized in the South. Absent a popular mandate, some have resorted to states of exception; others, to grasping more tightly to the Shield of the Americas and the “collaborations” it proffers with US forces. But the fact that so much of this can be traced to one man behind the curtain is telling. Cerimedo, of course, will be discarded and replaced; the line of former clients and compadres vying to distance themselves from him has already formed. But the house of cards that is the Latin American far right is swaying on its flimsy foundations: the rot of its digital magician has come to symbolize the rot at the heart of its project.

articles.title: The Human Soul of the Fight to Control AI
articles.author: Daniele G. Palmer
articles.content: During World War II, bomber pilots would tell each other, “if you’re taking flak, you’re over the target.” Don’t demur, you’ve struck a nerve. Opposition, at times, isn’t all that bad a sign — if anything, it could point to something good, or at least true. Judged by that standard, the reception of Pope Leo XIV’s pronouncement on artificial Intelligence has been curious. Some have fought over its account of just war theory; others have questioned its denial of machine sentience. Yet its diagnosis of the politics AI relies on, and the fixes needed to guard against it, has gone almost entirely unchallenged, especially among technologists. In a recent article for the Financial Times , theologian and AI sceptic Carmody Grey insists that Leo’s Magnifica Humanitas is unique. It not only represents the voice of “17.8 per cent of the world’s population,” Grey writes, but focuses on AI’s users more than the technology itself: to the humans whose dignity AI risks undercutting. Rather than offering any proposal or suggestion, Grey suggests, it offers a “style or approach” that surpasses “the narrow menu of contemporary moral thought. . . . and frames the ethics of AI as downstream of much deeper orientations regarding the purpose of human life.” But is this true? Part of the problem is about process. The broad-based consultation inaugurated under Pope Francis was not carried over into the making of Magnifica Humanitas . And it shows. While the long-standing Catholic anxiety about social fragmentation remains, it has been pushed toward the margins of the argument. This leaves Leo with a critique of capitalism that is less institutionally specific than those offered by previous popes: structural injustices are clearly identified, but the organized social forces capable of confronting them are much harder to find. Leo’s church may be yet to be captured, but its political ambivalence may unintentionally weaken the church’s institutional role in the fight against the effects of AI and the splintered society on which it relies. Unless carefully implemented, Magnifica Humanitas may give rise to a Catholicism less able to resist the social world embodied by the technologies of today. The Silent Work of Millions But first the good news. Or, better, the bad news Leo gets right. We find ourselves at a crossroads, Magnifica Humanitas stresses: either we create a new Tower of Babel and are crushed under our own hubris, or we rebuild a new Jerusalem from its ruins, one that can “safeguard the human person in the time of AI.” The Pope’s letter recognizes, at least, that today’s technologies represent a challenge, and one that’s not neutral. While AI may not necessarily be antagonistic to humanity, it emerges from worlds and minds that don’t have a firm grip on what dignity and the “common good” demand. “Each phase of progress,” the letter reads, reveals an “ambiguity of tools that can cause harm when not oriented toward the good.” This may emerge by falsely imputing large-language models (LLMs) qualities — feelings and consciousness — that they don’t have. Leo is keen to deny AI any sentience; he did so even when Chris Olah, one of Anthropic’s cofounders, was present at Magnifica Humanitas ’s launch in Rome onMay 25. At the press conference, Olah insisted on finding “evidence of introspection: we find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief and unease.” Yet for Leo, “nothing in the world of AI is immaterial or magical.” Rather, the problem is also material. AI is part of a new economy that plunders the spoils of old colonizers, Leo insists. And, in the process, it creates a new cadre of the poor and exploited: from data labelers and content moderators to those engaged in the harsher work of extracting the materials necessary for hardware, today’s technologies and the industries built on them rely on the “silent work of millions.” Its cause is as anthropological as it is political. Many of those involved in AI’s development are beholden to transhumanist and posthumanist ideas, which see technology’s role as engineering away the limits and frictions of the human condition. In the name of progress, of augmenting human performance and capabilities, Leo warns, “the human being is treated as something to be perfected or surpassed.” As a result, “it becomes easier to accept that some lives are less useful, less desirable or less worthy.” And for some, the sacrifice of others becomes necessary. This vision is bound to thrive in a network of checks and balances that has so far proven ineffective. Today’s technologies exist in a world in which, on Magnifica Humanitas ’s telling, the state no longer rules supreme. Instead, it is “major economic and technological actors” who “exercise de facto power.” They control knowledge and the data we produce (and that they farm) and wield the authority that comes with actually making decisions. And because of this, these “companies and platforms” have a near-totalizing presence in our lives, defining society’s “conditions of access, rules of visibility, forms of interaction and even economic opportunities.” Collaborative Movements What’s to be done? On this, Leo is less scathing. And he’s not all that clear, either. One suggestion is to embody a culture of limits, restraining those urges AI feeds, as well as placing guardrails on the technology as it develops. But while the objects of vigilance are clear enough, the institutional politics of imposing these limits is much less so. Similarly ambiguous is the “culture of shared responsibility” the letter calls on “all people of goodwill” to assume. While Leo does point to civil society’s many “communities,” from trade unions to universities, the language adopted is too capacious to mean much. This produces a vision of politics without a clear account of how these various organized constituencies operate. Nor are we given much sense of how they’re to acquire the leverage, or build the kinds of alliances, needed to combat the concentration of power. Previous popes were more precise. Catholic social thought, since the late nineteenth century, didn’t just diagnose modernity but also charted a path through it. For Leo XIII, who was Pope from 1878 to 1903, it ran through civil society, especially trade unions — bodies that could answer democracy’s call for participation while protecting workers from market forces. The commitment held, unevenly, into the next century: watching states capitulate in the interwar period, Pius XI called for an alliance between unions and local parishes, despite his reticence toward “organizations of Socialists and Communists,” reasoning that, given their increasingly overlapping membership rolls, Catholics and socialists would have to work together. Pope Francis was no different. When still archbishop of Buenos Aires, he forged an alliance with the movimientos populares , championing their fight for tierra , techo, y trabajo (land, a roof, and work). This continued when he moved to Rome: strengthening social movements and associations formed the heart of his pontificate. They were also to be brought into the church’s decision-making processes, in the Vatican as well as locally. This culminated, if only anecdotally, in an overlooked letter he wrote in support of a union’s cleaners’ branch in East London. Francis’s advocacy for the grassroots led to a slew of global meetings in which lay leaders and association members became co-constitutive of what Catholicism thought and did about society. What Magnifica Humanitas has to say about our institutions is less pronounced. Most immediately, it foregoes detailed advice. And this wouldn’t be too much of a problem if it didn’t present a flattened picture of civil society: unions and associations are clustered alongside other groups, with the slightly vague encouragement to find solutions at national as well as local levels. And in a style reminiscent of corporate feel-good statements, Leo calls for “well-structured models, local initiatives, progressive redistribution and new rights of access to essential goods.” It may have to do with the vision of politics Magnifica Humanitas holds to. For example, unions are invited into “collaborative efforts” with governments and business; yet this mistakes the order of operations: regulation presupposes the very organized social power it’s meant to check, and that power has to be built before it can be deployed, not summoned by the same process it’s supposed to constrain. AI, moreover, isn’t a fixed target waiting to be regulated: its categories keep shifting under use. What’s needed is less a seat at the table than the prior, slower work of reforging the bonds that make a table possible at all — anticipatory, even prefigurative, rather than reactive. But the theory isn’t the only problem. Despite being involved in the initial stages of the church’s reflection on AI — which largely began under Francis — the very bodies that represent the people, from social movements to trade unions, were not part of the process when Leo took over. Magnifica Humanitas did not come out of any broader consultative process — the document, in fact, was released earlier than many expected — with collaborators principally being academics and clerics. This is odd. More forcefully than any previous social encyclical, the document sees discernment as the motor force behind Catholic social thought. Yet who Leo thinks should do this is telling: though he speaks of the “whole People of God”, he gives pastors and theologians a privileged role in making sense of the “voices of our times.” Unlike what Francis attempted to embody, Magnifica Humanitas imagines an all-too-benevolent caste of interpreters through whom communities are heard, rather than pushing for them to be intimately involved in the church’s discernment from the start. Methodological Individualism This might not just be an oversight. Leo’s Augustinian emphasis on the personal over the popular helps to explain why; it may also be tied to his training as a priest in the United States, where ecclesial power was never wholly antagonistic to business — and never terribly keen to issue calls of solidarity. For most of its history, Catholic social thought professed a deeper vision of human life: one in which individuals exist as parts of a whole. Society is not merely an aggregation of many interests, nor a spontaneous entity that overrides its constitutive parts: meaning, neither the units liberals wanted to herd and administer nor the tribes that would stampede the nationalists into office. Rather, it is the result of the deliberate and very difficult task of forging and maintaining bonds and institutions. Sociability, to use a term previous popes reached for, was a gift to be treasured and guarded. Its opposite, social fragmentation, was one of modernity’s greatest threats. In its own way, this formed the core of Francis’s effort to rebuild practices of “social friendship” within and outside the church. This culminated in the clunkily named “synodal way,” a concern with the building blocks of fellowship and coexistence. His answer to individualism was, therefore, not simply to remind individuals that they belonged to one another, but to create practices and institutions through which they might actually do so. Magnifica Humanitas represents a shift in this sense. While it doesn’t abandon the fear of the “individualistic and technical view of humanity,” the “network of relationships” that Leo proposes is a bit too similar to the “networked individualism” of apparent proximity that scholars believe AI produces: a social body without any real substance. In fact, much of Magnifica Humanitas ’s diagnosis is markedly centered on the person: a struggle between rightly and wrongly ordered loves, between one directed at God and one’s neighbor or the “exclusive love of the self.” All this, Leo writes, “begins within each one of us.” Even communal life, he stresses, mainly acquires meaning insofar as it allows and guarantees individuals to flourish, personal freedom to be guarded, and private enterprise to be supported. This may be a question of emphasis, but its implications are significant. There is a danger that problems of social organization become too readily issues of personal orientation. Magnifica Humanitas is aware that AI can lead to isolation, even distorting and manipulating the relationships we have. But it stops short of seeing how its antidote is greater, deeper, and stronger practices of association and not just better governance. While only mentioned in passing, Leo’s sense of individualism, as a result, appears primarily as a malformed way of seeing the human person: not, that is, the structural architecture of the social world that we inhabit. This explains the letter’s attitude toward capitalism, as well as the liberalism that Catholics once demonized. While Leo remains critical of the underpinnings of today’s political economy, he has shifted the church’s posture toward its remedies. What will redirect our institutions toward dignity and the common good, it appears, has less to do with the painful task of rebuilding social bonds and practices than the Catholic social tradition once thought. For all its talk of better governance, only this would allow these rules to come into being and to be maintained. Social Thought? When Leo chose his name, he signaled to the world that Catholic social thought would be the centerpiece of his pontificate. This can hardly be denied. Barely a year after his election, his first doctrinal pronouncement has been on society. Yet beneath the continuity lies a change, and one that is not merely gradual. The tone as well as the substance of Magnifica Humanitas , when read against other titles in the genre, corresponds to a transformation of outlook. The description Leo offers of civil society, to use a term dear to technologists, functionally mirrors that of his predecessors. But this isn’t enough. In her Financial Times article, Grey references the philosopher John Searle’s “Chinese Room” thought-experiment: just because an output is produced on command doesn’t mean that there’s someone, somewhere, who subjectively understands what it’s been asked. This can be applied to Magnifica Humanitas . Though it contains the familiar language of solidarity and subsidiarity, what remains unclear is the subject that will make them a reality. To avoid becoming Catholic social thought’s own Chinese Room, the church must have more than the right vocabulary: it will need to lend its support to the people and institutions through which sociability is actually built.

articles.title: The Israel Lobby Is Out of Control
articles.author: Eli Clifton
articles.content: In a year of record-breaking campaign spending by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and widespread popular revulsion at Donald Trump’s war on Iran, a deeply researched study of the Israel lobby couldn’t be timelier. Jacobin ’s Seth Ackerman spoke with investigative journalist Eli Clifton and veteran scholar Ian Lustick about their new book Israel’s Lobby : America in the Grip of a Foreign Power , which reveals how the lobby has not only warped Washington politics but accelerated Israel’s own ideological radicalization — and now threatens Americans’ civil liberties at home. Seth Ackerman Almost twenty years ago, the international relations scholars John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt wrote a very famous and very controversial book called The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy . Your book is in many ways a sequel to theirs. What made you decide the time was right for a book like this? Eli Clifton A lot has changed since 2007. Steve Walt and John Mearsheimer identified some of the global strategic costs that the lobby’s activities were imposing on Americans, and those have continued to amplify and magnify. But some of the other costs are more domestic in nature, and those were enabled by changes in our laws, which Steve and John could not have foreseen. In their book’s conclusion, they argued that support for a “no daylight” relationship with Israel was slowly seeping away. They identified that trend as having begun around 1999 or 2000, with the death of the Oslo Accords and the closing of the window on the two-state solution. And they predicted that that slow decline would be met by the rise of other institutions — such as J Street, Jewish Voice for Peace, and others — that would be able to advocate for a more normal and balanced US-Israel relationship and make it possible to wean US politics off the influence of the lobby. But in 2010, the Citizens United and SpeechNow decisions came down. That opened the floodgates of our campaign finance system. Starting in 2012, which was the first post– Citizens United election, when you look at who the biggest donors were, it was Sheldon Adelson and other pro-Israel billionaire megadonors. And they said very explicitly that they were doing this for Israel. So in the face of declining public support for Israel — which really accelerated post–October 7 across pretty much every demographic — that allowed them to create a stopgap. Alongside the money, there was also a strategic shift. The lobby stopped trying to counter arguments like those of Mearsheimer and Walt. Instead they moved to completely shut down debate, including by using the power of the state to shut down speech critical of Israel. We saw that with the withholding of hundreds of millions of dollars of federal funding from universities, often in research areas that have nothing to do with Israel or Palestine. Or in the attempts to deport green card holders simply because of their criticisms of a foreign country. So we’re now paying a domestic price in terms of our own civil liberties. That’s a key part of what has changed since their book came out. Seth Ackerman One of the arguments made by Mearsheimer and Walt twenty years ago was that the end of the Cold War eliminated the major rationale that had once been used to justify Israel’s privileged relationship with the United States. Would you say that the lobby then tried to turn Iran into the new Soviet Union — the new enemy that would make Israel indispensable to the United States? Ian Lustick Israel did present itself as a crucial ally against Soviet penetration of the Middle East, though that claim was never very convincing to experts. In the book, we report a fascinating natural experiment that proved how empty the claim was. In 1991, one of the leading international relations analysts, A. F. K. Organski, a University of Michigan professor, published a book called The $36 Billion Bargain , which argued that Israel was like a land-based aircraft carrier: it was so useful to the United States in its struggle against the Soviet Union that all the aid we gave to it was a bargain. And as part of his argument, he asked: How can we know this is true? Well, if the Soviet Union were to disappear and the Cold War were to end, we would see the aid drop. Now that’s exactly what happened right after his book was published. The Soviet Union disintegrated, and the Cold War ended. And what happened to aid to Israel? Absolutely nothing. It continued at exactly the same level. Which showed that aid to Israel was not a function of American strategic calculations. It was overwhelmingly a function of the domestic political power of Israel’s lobby in the United States. But the argument that Israel served US strategic interests was important to both Israel and its lobby. After the end of the Cold War, both needed a domain within which it could present itself as a crucial ally of the United States. Accordingly, during the global war on terror (GWOT), Israeli leaders said that their wars against Hezbollah or against the Palestinians in the West Bank were part of the US-led war on terror. But then the GWOT ended, and another domain was needed for Israel to present itself as America’s crucial ally. Benjamin Netanyahu chose Iran to play the role of mortal enemy of both Israel and the United States, replacing the war on terror, which had replaced the Soviet Union. But Netanyahu actually had great difficulty fomenting the combined US-Israeli attack on Iran that he wanted. Israel’s own security establishment opposed him, arguing that no, Iran was never going to attack Israel with a nuclear weapon. He also ran into a series of American presidents who all thought attacking Iran was a wacky idea. His demands for a war were successfully resisted until in Trump he found a president stupid enough — and a national security bureaucracy so drained of expertise and so incompetent — that he was able to essentially drag the United States into a war with Iran, a war which even Trump now probably thinks was a terrible mistake. But there’s a deeper reason why Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, has been on the warpath against Iran, Gaza, Syria, Lebanon — and why lately he’s been ginning up a crisis with Turkey. The deep reason for such a bellicose posture is that his governments have been unable to articulate a vision of peace in the Middle East that anybody in the region would be satisfied with. And since they don’t have any vision of peace, they have to rely completely on their ability to use military force at almost no risk, whether that’s in Lebanon or Iraq or Syria or Gaza or Iran. The other day we saw the Israeli Air Force bomb a base in Syria — not because there was a threat, but because there was potentially a threat, from Turkey or from the Syrian military. That is emblematic of the situation Israel has created for itself. If it can’t rely on diplomacy or negotiated compromises, it must rely on military force. But to rely on military force, it must be confident it can use that force without risk of significant casualties, or of escalation to the use of weapons of mass destruction. It therefore, in effect, insists on absolute air superiority and domination over the entire Middle East. And it has to insist that only it be permitted to have weapons of mass destruction. These are enormous demands. Remember, Iran is geographically bigger than Britain, France, and Germany combined. The threat from Iran is not that it will attack Israel with nuclear weapons. It’s that if there’s even a 1 percent possibility that Iran could escalate to the nuclear level, Israel would no longer be able to use force in the region without fearing escalation. That’s intolerable if you have no plan for peace, which the Netanyahu government has never had. That’s the deeper reason he’s focused so much on Iran and relies so heavily on military force. Seth Ackerman In your book, you argue that this strategic predicament is itself partly the result of the lobby’s power in the United States. Ian Lustick Yes. Originally, the lobby was only there to prevent pressure on Israel; it wasn’t out to change Israel, to make it into this fanatical right-wing state. But by insisting that aid to Israel be enormous in scope and unconditional in its delivery, the lobby made it essentially impossible, or at least extremely difficult, for moderate candidates to win elections in Israel. Because everything they said about what would happen if Israel alienated the United States — that it would pressure Israel into a deal worse than it could get if it adopted a reasonable position before that pressure — turned out to be false. This is what happens to a country that has too much externally supplied political capital. If you were a politician in Israel, you learned that you had to pander to people’s fantasies and fears, and there was no real cost to it. But there was a tremendous cost to talking rationally about the predicament Israel would eventually find itself in. I can list all these wonderful Israeli politicians — Shulamit Aloni, Haim Ramon, Yossi Sarid, Yossi Beilin — all of these people who could have been prime minister, and wanted to be prime minister but didn’t succeed, and couldn’t succeed, because of the lobby’s hammerlock on US policy toward Israel and the Palestinians. Seth Ackerman In other words, many Israelis used to assume that if push ever came to shove, America would save Israel from itself by stepping in and restraining it. Ian Lustick Yes. And that was specifically the problem with Joe Biden. He didn’t play the role the Israeli military always expects the United States to play. When Time magazine interviewed me early in the Gaza war, they asked: When will the war end? I said, “I can tell you exactly when it will end. It’s the same as in every war. It will end when the United States tells Israel it has to end. Until that happens, the war will continue.” And Biden just wouldn’t say it. Trump more or less said it and it stopped (or at least, a certain version of war stopped). But it went on for years — far, far longer than it ever should have. It was ridiculous. The Israeli military never imagined that an American president would allow it to run so wild for so long. Seth Ackerman What about the liberal part of the American pro-Israel establishment? They seem to be in a pretty complicated political situation right now. Do you think they’ve figured out a way forward? Eli Clifton One thing you see them doing is clinging, in a rather desperate, disingenuous way, to the fig leaf of a notion that the Israel they would like to be associated with somehow still exists, or is right around the corner. So if Netanyahu is removed, somehow this rightward shift will come to an end and Israel will go back to being like what it was, I guess, pre-1967. When push comes to shove, politicians across the Democratic Party say: “I believe in a two-state solution.” And that’s a dangerous thing for them to be saying because it’s simply not rooted in any facts on the ground. The window has closed for that possibility, as desirable as it might have been. So I think the way a lot of them are coping with it, to put it pretty bluntly, is through delusion, and through misrepresenting to their constituents what is possible and what the facts are on the ground. Ian Lustick Let me push that a little further. I published a book on this in 2019, Paradigm Lost: From Two-State Solution to One-State Reality . Even then it had long since been impossible to imagine political scenarios by which a two-state solution could be achieved. Those stopped being produced in the 1990s when Oslo ended. But it’s been a safe political harbor to claim that a negotiated two-state arrangement is still possible. It’s been safe for Israeli centrists who don’t want to admit they prefer apartheid to democracy. And it’s been safe for Democratic and other politicians in the United States, who are able to say: “I’m for a two-state solution. Don’t blame me, progressives.” And meanwhile they can also say to the lobby: “Don’t criticize me — even Netanyahu once said he was for a two-state solution.” As Eli said, it’s a fig leaf. So where is the future? I would say you have to change the time frame of your analysis. Back when we used to think of a two-state solution as being plausible, we were thinking in what I call strategic time. Strategic time is like two to five years, the time frame when you actually might accomplish something in this kind of arena. We have to shift from strategic time to geological time. Geological time in politics is like thirty to sixty years. How does a country like Israel democratize? It’s not the same as how Romania democratized: you shoot the dictator, and the next day, it’s a democracy. That’s not how democratization works in cases like, say, America when blacks were for generations excluded from politics, or Irish Catholics in Britain, or blacks in South Africa, or women in all western industrial democracies. That kind of democratization takes fifty to a hundred years. Seth Ackerman But isn’t there a danger that, in adopting that frame, you inadvertently give apologists for the status quo an excuse to do nothing? If progress can only happen in geological time, what’s the urgency of doing anything today? Ian Lustick It’s not going to happen tomorrow. But we should call the bluff of those in Israel who say they want to keep the territories Israel occupied in 1967. When you look at the West Bank annexation bills in the Knesset, none of them talk about immediate annexation of all the people and territory. They are actually afraid of really annexing the territories. They prefer to maintain the fiction that they have not already been permanently absorbed. Seth Ackerman In the short term, the lobby seems to be hoping that after the elections in October there will be a new government — presumably led by Gadi Eisenkot — that presents a kinder, gentler face to the American public. Could that work? Ian Lustick Maybe. But it won’t last. Remember who Gadi Eisenkot is. Compared to Netanyahu, he may look like a reasonable guy who’s focused on reality and not fantasy, and not on pandering to the worst prejudices of his audience. But he’s also the progenitor of the “Dahiya doctrine.” That’s the doctrine named after a neighborhood in Beirut that Israel completely destroyed, not just to kill combatants but to destroy all the civilian infrastructure around them. What we saw in Gaza was the application of that doctrine. So let’s not think too ambitiously about what Eisenkot has to offer. I think the most interesting question about the upcoming election is whether Eisenkot will even be able to form a government without aligning himself with Arab-majority parties. The Ra’am party will now have a Jewish member of its Knesset slate, so it won’t be a pure Arab party anymore, but it still won’t be a “Zionist party” as Israelis define it. And the way Netanyahu frames it, only traitors would form a government with the support of non-Zionist parties. (Though of course, he himself tried to do that in the past). But looking at it in terms of geological time, what interests me is the precedent of Arab-Jewish cooperation — even right-wing cooperation with Arabs — that presages the possibility that at some point in the future, significant numbers of Jews will see advantages for themselves in West Bank and Gaza Palestinians being able to vote. Will we have an election outcome where no one can form a government unless the coalition includes Arabs? And how will the Israeli political system react to that? To me, that’s more important than the question of how long Eisenkot will be able to keep putting lipstick on the pig. I’m more interested in whether this election will force the country to move toward Jewish-Arab political alliances. Seth Ackerman I asked earlier about Mearsheimer and Walt’s book. Twenty years ago, their book became a kind of literary scandal. Publications refused to publish their work, nasty reviews accused them of all kinds of terrible things. How would you compare the reaction you’ve gotten to your book so far? Eli Clifton It’s very different. We’re no longer in a world where you have to debate whether or not the lobby exists. When you look at the pushback against Steve and John, that’s unfortunately where they had to fight a lot of their battles: it was about whether the lobby exists at all, and whether saying it exists is somehow antisemitic. And that’s no longer the world we’re in. It’s pretty well established. I mean, I have this website I maintain — israelslobby.com — which tracks Federal Election Comission records on pro-Israel Super PACs in real time. Right now I think they’ve raised $160 million in this political cycle. That probably means they’re going to have raised $250 million just for these midterms. A quarter of a billion dollars — that’s a lot of money for a special interest for a foreign country to raise and spend. So the lobby objectively exists. That’s not something we have to debate anymore. It’s also in the headlines. We’ve been fortunate with the timing of the book, because this is very much a part of the public debate right now, particularly with the Gaza war, the Iran war, and the midterms. It’s a top-of-mind issue for voters in a way that foreign policy issues generally aren’t. Of course, that’s also the downside: a lot of people are talking about this now. So we’re trying to bring something new to the table, to contextualize how we got to this moment. This isn’t just a current affairs book. It’s looking at the historical record of how Israel’s lobby became what it is today and what that has meant, in terms of lost diplomatic opportunities for the United States, in terms of lost resources, but also in terms of the measurable domestic price of crackdowns on civil liberties, antisemitism witch hunts, efforts to curtail speech, particularly at universities. In that respect, this is a scarier moment than 2007.
